name: Trifarotene (Aklief)

lead: Trifarotene (Aklief) is a prescription topical retinoid from Galderma, approved by the FDA in October 2019 for acne in people aged 9 and older. It is used for clearer skin on the face, chest and back, and users discuss it as a step between tretinoin and isotretinoin.

It selectively activates retinoic acid receptor gamma, the most common receptor type in skin. Like other topical retinoids it normalizes skin-cell turnover, which clears clogged pores and calms breakouts. Its pivotal trials enrolled people with acne on both face and trunk, giving it rigorous truncal data other topical retinoids lack, and later phase 4 trials have looked at post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and acne scars.

paras: It is a once-daily cream applied in the evening to affected areas, prescribed by a clinician and used alongside a moisturizer and sunscreen. Acne improvement is judged over weeks to months of consistent use. It carries an acne approval only, not an anti-aging one.

The most common reactions are application-site irritation, itching and sunburn. The label advises moisturizer, reduced frequency if needed, and sun protection. Trial data have not identified a pregnancy-related risk, but case reports with other topical retinoids describe birth defects like those from oral retinoids. It is prescription-only.

chain: Clearer skin on face and trunk
angle.text: Aklief is a prescription retinoid cream that selectively activates RAR-gamma to clear pores and calm breakouts, giving clearer skin on the face, chest and back. It is FDA-approved for acne and tested in large vehicle-controlled trials; it carries no anti-aging approval.

lead: Trifarotene, sold as Aklief (a 0.005% cream), is a prescription topical retinoid developed by Galderma that selectively activates retinoic acid receptor gamma (RAR-gamma) and is classed as a fourth-generation retinoid. [1][2] The US FDA approved it in October 2019 for the topical treatment of acne vulgaris in patients 9 years of age and older. [1][3] For appearance, its payoff is clearer skin: fewer inflamed spots and blackheads on the face, and on the shoulders, chest and back, which are the areas where people most often wear exposed clothing. [3][4]

Its distinguishing feature is clinical data on truncal acne. Reviewers state that, unlike earlier topical retinoids, it is the first with rigorous trial data on safety and efficacy for acne on the trunk as well as the face. [5][4] Later phase 4 work has looked at what acne leaves behind, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (dark marks) and atrophic acne scars, which are the lasting skin-quality problems many people actually want to fix. [6][7] It is approved for acne only; it does not carry an anti-aging indication, and Grokipedia notes that support for anti-aging use is limited and mostly preclinical. [3][2]

In looksmaxxing forums, trifarotene appears mostly as a prescription step between older topical retinoids such as tretinoin and oral isotretinoin for acne, discussed by teenagers and young adults weighing their options. [8] In the US it is prescription-only, and Wikipedia lists the same status in Canada, the UK and Australia. [3][9]
infobox: October 2019 (US); Canada November 2019; Australia January 2021 (per Wikipedia)
Face and upper trunk (chest, shoulders, back) [3][4]

paras: The label indication is topical treatment of acne vulgaris. [3] People use it to treat active breakouts on both the face and the upper trunk; the label describes one pump for the face and two for the upper trunk, applied once daily in the evening to clean dry skin, avoiding eyes, lips and mucous membranes. [3]

Phase 4 studies have examined its effect on acne-induced dark marks in skin of color and on the development of atrophic scars, which extend its use from controlling spots to improving how skin looks afterwards. [6][10][7]

Guidelines from the American Academy of Dermatology make a strong recommendation for topical retinoids in acne in general. [11] A 2026 European update of the EuroGuiDerm guideline prioritised a question on which patients should receive new topical treatments such as trifarotene and clascoterone. [12] Trifarotene has received orphan designation for congenital ichthyosis, with a phase 2 lamellar ichthyosis study in the registry, but it is not approved for that condition. [13][2]

The label describes trifarotene as an RAR agonist with particular activity at the gamma subtype, which modulates genes involved in cell differentiation and inflammation, and states that the exact process by which it improves acne is unknown. [3] RAR-gamma is the most common RAR isoform in skin, and the selectivity is said to account for efficacy at low concentration. [5] Like other topical retinoids, it increases keratinocyte differentiation and decreases proliferation, which reduces hyperkeratinization, and retinoids have also been shown to inhibit inflammatory pathways. [5]

Its design from a structure-based approach, aimed at making a RAR-gamma-selective agonist with a wider safety margin than earlier RAR-beta/gamma dual agonists, was reported in 2018. [14] Reviewers place it as the most recent of four retinoid generations, after tretinoin and the later adapalene and tazarotene era. [15]

Systemic exposure is low. In a label pharmacokinetic study of 19 adults applying the cream daily for 29 days, drug levels were quantifiable in only 7 subjects, plasma protein binding was about 99.9% and the half-life was 2 to 9 hours. [3] Nonclinical and human pharmacology data and a clinical pharmacology and safety report have been published. [16][17]

Pivotal trials. Two phase 3, double-blind, randomized, vehicle-controlled 12-week studies of once-daily trifarotene 50 micrograms per gram cream enrolled participants aged 9 and older with moderate facial and truncal acne; primary endpoints were Investigator's Global Assessment success on the face (clear or almost clear with at least a 2-grade improvement) and changes in inflammatory and non-inflammatory lesion counts, with truncal success as a secondary endpoint. [4] One of the two registered studies enrolled 1,208 participants. [18] The label reports 2,420 participants across the two studies. [3]

Results. At week 12 the label reports facial IGA success of 29.4% versus 19.5% for vehicle in study 1 and 42.3% versus 25.7% in study 2, and trunk success of 35.7% versus 25.0% and 42.6% versus 29.9%. Mean reductions in facial inflammatory lesions were 54.4% versus 44.8% and 66.2% versus 51.2%, and in facial non-inflammatory lesions 49.7% versus 35.7% and 57.7% versus 43.9%. [3] A review summarising these data describes trifarotene as efficacious in reducing comedones and papules/pustules, and as safe and well tolerated. [5]

Long-term data. A long-term study (registered with 453 participants) and its published report examined safety and efficacy over a longer duration in moderate facial and truncal acne. [19][20] Grokipedia reports that in a 52-week open-label extension, success rates rose to about 65% on the face and 67% on the trunk, with 2.9% discontinuing for adverse events; this figure is the encyclopedia's summary rather than a value checked against the paper. [2]

Hyperpigmentation and scars. A phase 4 trial (LEAP) in acne-induced post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in skin of color, run with a skincare routine including UV protection, was published in 2024, and a later qualitative interview study reported that trifarotene-treated patients in this trial had faster improvement in hyperpigmentation than those on vehicle cream at week 12. [6][10] A phase 4 controlled study reported that trifarotene reduced the risk of atrophic acne scars. [7]

Comparisons. A trial of tazarotene 0.045% lotion compared its irritation potential with adapalene 0.3% gel and trifarotene 0.005% cream in two studies. [21] Narrative reviews place trifarotene among newer acne therapies alongside clascoterone and sarecycline. [22][15] Registered studies compare a trifarotene 0.005% cream with Aklief. [23]
Cosmetic and anti-aging outcomes. No studies have tested trifarotene for photoaging or wrinkles.

The most common adverse reactions (1% or more) are application-site irritation (7.5%), sunburn (2.6%) and application-site itching (2.4%). [3] Local tolerability signs are common but mostly mild to moderate: at the worst point after baseline, the label reports facial erythema in 30.6% mild, 28.4% moderate and 6.2% severe, with scaling, dryness and stinging or burning following a similar pattern, highest in week 1 on the face and weeks 2 to 4 on the trunk. [3]

Warnings cover skin irritation, for which the label suggests a moisturizer from the start and reduced frequency if needed, and ultraviolet exposure, where the label advises minimizing sunlight and using sunscreen and protective clothing. [3]

Pregnancy. The label notes that clinical-trial pregnancies did not identify a risk of major birth defects or miscarriage, but that case reports exist of birth defects similar to those after oral retinoids in women exposed to other topical retinoids; it states these do not establish a pattern. [3] Wikipedia lists use in pregnancy as contraindicated because of the teratogenic risk of retinoids as a class. [9]

Galderma Research and Development developed trifarotene, and it received its first global approval in the USA in October 2019. [1] Grokipedia reports that Galderma's structure-based design programme produced the compound, which was coded CD5789, and that the FDA gave orphan designation for congenital ichthyosis in 2014. [2][14]

Wikipedia lists Canadian approval in November 2019 for face and/or trunk acne in people aged 12 and older, a decentralised European labelling approval covering 16 countries in December 2019, and Australian approval in January 2021. [9] Reviews describe a lineage of topical retinoids from tretinoin (FDA-approved 1971) through successive generations to RAR-gamma-selective agents. [15]

On looksmax.org, a young poster says their dermatologist recommended Aklief as a last resort before isotretinoin after tretinoin did not work, and that they chose it partly because of concerns about isotretinoin's effects on growth; replies include support for the choice and a comment that most topical retinoids are 'cope' for long-term remission. [8] The poster's claims about isotretinoin are the poster's own and are not assessed in this article.

In skincare discussion, trifarotene is placed in the ladder of acne treatments that runs from benzoyl peroxide and adapalene to tretinoin, tazarotene, trifarotene and isotretinoin; AAD guidelines treat topical retinoids as a core therapy and reserve oral isotretinoin for severe, scarring or treatment-resistant acne. [11][8]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, Aklief appears in acne threads as a prescription option short of isotretinoin, especially among younger posters. [8]

claims.claim: Aklief is a reasonable step before isotretinoin when tretinoin has not worked.
Trifarotene works on face and body acne.
Topical retinoids are not enough for long-term remission.
It fades acne marks and prevents scarring.
It is a more tolerable retinoid than older ones.

timeline.event: FDA approves tretinoin, the first topical retinoid for acne. [15]

Pivotal phase 3 study of trifarotene versus vehicle registered. [18]
Structure-based design of CD5789 and its pharmacology reported. [16][14]
Phase 3 results published; FDA approves Aklief on October 2019 for acne in patients 9 and older; Canada and Europe follow. [4][1][9]
Phase 4 study on atrophic acne scars published. [7]
Phase 4 LEAP study in acne-induced post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in skin of color published. [6]
